AI Foundations · Lesson 6 · 30 minutes

Many weak trees, one strong model

Random forests, gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost: what they do, and which to pick.

Press N for presenter lines · F fullscreen · arrows to move

1906, a country fair in England

787 people guessed the weight of an ox

1 Most individual guesses were badly off
2 The middle guess of the crowd: 1,207 lb. The truth: 1,198 lb (under 1% off)
3 Why? Each person's error was different, so the errors cancelled out

The one formula behind every ensemble

error spread of the average = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/n

n = number of models

more models shrink the second part toward zero

ρ = how alike they are

the first part never shrinks: if all models make the same mistakes, averaging can't help

Why? So a good ensemble needs two things: many models, and models that make different mistakes. Every method today is a different trick for those two goals.

Two families of ensembles

Bagging → Random forest

• many deep trees, built in parallel
• each sees a different random sample
• average them
• fixes variance (instability)

Boosting → XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost

• many small trees, built one after another
• each fixes the previous trees' mistakes
• add them up
• fixes bias (too simple)

Part A · Bagging = bootstrap aggregating

Give every tree a different sample

1 Draw 5,634 customers with replacement: some appear twice, ~37% not at all
2 Grow a full, deep tree on that sample
3 Repeat hundreds of times; average their probabilities
Why? Each tree overfits, but to different noise, because it saw different customers. Averaging cancels the noise and keeps the pattern.

Our data: a crowd of bad trees beats one good tree

Why? One full tree: 0.66. Average 25 of them: 0.82. After ~100 trees the curve is flat: more trees never make a forest overfit, they only cost time.

Random forest = bagging + one more trick

1 Problem: every tree asks "month-to-month?" first, so the trees look alike (high ρ)
2 Trick: at each split, a tree may only look at a random handful of features (√34 ≈ 6)
3 Some trees are forced to find other good questions → more different mistakes
Why? Measured on our data: average correlation between trees fell 0.374 → 0.356, and test AUC with 200 trees rose 0.817 → 0.825.

Random forest settings: all the options

SettingMeaningOur CV AUCAdvice
n_estimatorsnumber of treesflat after ~100–200more is never worse, only slower: use 300–500
min_samples_leafsmallest leaf allowed1 → 0.826 · 20 → 0.848the knob that mattered most here
max_featuresfeatures tried per split√ → 0.848 · all → 0.841default √ is usually right
max_depthcap on depthsimilar to leaf sizeuse one of the two, not both
class_weightre-weights the rare classchanges calibrationprefer threshold tuning (Lesson 3)
Best choice: 300–500 trees, tune min_samples_leaf (5–50), keep max_features = √. Forests are the most forgiving model you will meet.

A free test set: out-of-bag scoring

The idea

each tree never saw ~37% of customers. Score every customer using only the trees that didn't see them.

Our numbers

OOB AUC 0.848 · 5-fold CV 0.848 · test 0.845

Why? Same answer as cross-validation, at zero extra training cost. With big data or slow models, OOB saves you 5× the work.

Remember the instability problem? Solved.

Why? Retrain on a different half of the data: a single full tree changes 25.6% of answers; a forest changes only 3.7%. Averaging is a stabiliser.

Part B · Boosting

Each new tree studies the mistakes of the team so far

prediction = start + η·tree₁ + η·tree₂ + η·tree₃ + …
Why? Start with a simple guess (the average). Fit a small tree to what's still wrong (the residuals). Add a fraction η of it. Repeat. Like a student who reviews only the questions they got wrong.

Watch boosting build a prediction (stumps, η = 0.5)

Why? Each stump alone is useless: one yes/no question. Added together, 20 of them trace the curve. Weak learners → strong model.

Why "gradient" boosting? Lesson 4 again

1 Lesson 4: gradient descent nudges weights downhill on the error
2 Boosting nudges the predictions downhill: each tree points in the direction that lowers the error
3 For squared error that direction is exactly the residual; for churn it's the slope of log loss
Why? So η is a learning rate, the same idea as in Lesson 4: too big overshoots, too small needs many steps.

Learning rate × number of trees: tested on our data

Why? η = 1.0: best after 11 trees, then overfits fast. η = 0.03: needs 291 trees but reaches the lowest error. Smaller steps = more trees = slightly better, and gentler overfitting.

So how many trees? Let the data say stop

1 Hold out a validation set
2 Add trees; after each one, check validation error
3 No improvement for 100 rounds → stop, keep the best. Our XGBoost stopped itself at 337 trees.
Best choice: small learning rate (0.03–0.1) + a large tree budget + early stopping. You never tune n_estimators by hand again.

Boosting settings: all the options

Setting (XGBoost / LightGBM name)ControlsTypical range
learning_ratestep size0.01–0.1 (with early stopping)
n_estimatorsnumber of treeslarge; early stopping decides
max_depth / num_leavessize of each tree (how many features can interact)depth 3–8 / 8–64 leaves
min_child_weight / min_child_samplessmallest leafraise on small or noisy data
subsample, colsample_bytreerandom rows / columns per tree (bagging inside boosting)0.6–0.9
reg_lambda, reg_alphaRidge / Lasso penalty on leaf values (Lesson 4)0–10
Best choice: tune in this order: learning rate + early stopping → tree size → leaf size → subsampling → penalties. Use a search tool (Optuna or random search) with cross-validation.

Five boosting libraries: what makes each special

LibrarySpecial ideaTest AUCTrain time*
sklearn GradientBoostingthe classic textbook algorithm0.8457.6 s
sklearn HistGradientBoostingbins numbers into 255 buckets → fast; handles missing values0.8461.1 s
XGBoost (2014)uses curvature (2nd derivative) + built-in penalties; the Kaggle legend0.8480.9 s
LightGBM (2017)grows the most useful leaf first; very fast on big data0.8480.9 s
CatBoost (2017)handles text categories natively, without one-hot; strong with little tuning0.84713.9 s

*5-fold CV + final fit, 2 CPU cores, same light tuning for all

Best choice: XGBoost or LightGBM as the default; CatBoost when you have many categorical columns (cities, product IDs). The top three are within 0.001: tuning and features matter more than the library.

The full leaderboard on our churn data

The trap in that chart

XGBoost on defaults scored 0.829: worse than one tree

Train AUCTest AUC
XGBoost defaults (depth 6, η 0.3, 100 trees)0.9840.829
XGBoost tuned (depth 3, η 0.03, leaf ≥5, subsample)0.8730.848
Why? Defaults are built for big data. On 5,634 customers they memorise (train 0.98). Big train-test gap = overfitting, exactly Lesson 2. "I used XGBoost" means nothing without tuning and validation.

The honest result: how much did all this buy us?

ModelTest AUCLeavers in our top 141 picks
Single tuned tree0.833102
Logistic regression (same features)0.840105
Random forest0.845107
XGBoost (tuned)0.848108
Why? Boosting beat logistic regression by +0.008 AUC (95% bootstrap interval: +0.000 to +0.016): real, but small; 3 more leavers caught in the top 10%. Why small? This dataset is simple: 7k rows, 19 columns, mostly smooth effects. Boosting wins big on large, messy data with many interacting features.

Can we combine the winners? Voting & stacking

MethodHowCV AUCTest AUCTime
XGBoost alone—0.8490.8480.9 s
Soft votingaverage LR + forest + LightGBM probabilities0.8510.8478 s
Stackinga logistic model learns how to weigh them0.8500.84748 s
Best choice: in production, one well-tuned boosting model. Voting/stacking add complexity and latency for ~0.002 here; they are for competitions, or when models are truly different (e.g. text model + table model).

Bagging vs boosting: side by side

Random forest (bagging)Gradient boosting
Fixesvariance (instability)bias (too simple), and variance with tuning
Treesdeep, independent, parallelsmall, sequential
More treesnever overfitscan overfit → early stopping
Tuning neededlittle (very forgiving)more (but rewards it)
Typical accuracy on tablesvery goodusually the best
Free extrasOOB scorenative missing values / categories (LightGBM, CatBoost)

Which model should you reach for?

SituationReach for
Business / tabular data, want top accuracyLightGBM or XGBoost, tuned with early stopping
Many text categories (city, product, store)CatBoost
Quick, robust baseline with almost no tuningrandom forest
Must explain every weight; regulated (credit, health)logistic regression, or boosting + SHAP explanations
Images, audio, textneural networks (Part II)
Best choice: always train logistic regression first as a baseline; ship boosting only if it beats the baseline by a margin that matters to the business.

Say this in an interview

Q "Bagging vs boosting?" → bagging averages deep independent trees to cut variance; boosting adds small trees sequentially, each fitting the gradient of the loss, to cut bias
Q "Why random features in a forest?" → to de-correlate the trees; the average only cancels errors that differ (ρ in the formula)
Q "Can more trees overfit?" → forest: no. Boosting: yes; use a small learning rate + early stopping

Bridge to modern AI

The crowd idea is everywhere in deep learning

1 Dropout randomly switches off neurons while training: it acts like averaging many thinned networks
2 Self-consistency: ask an LLM the same question several times and take the majority answer; it often improves reasoning
3 Residual connections in transformers: each layer adds a correction to what came before, a cousin of boosting's "add a fix" step

Check yourself · 1 of 5

Why does averaging 500 overfitting trees give a good model?

AnswerEach tree overfits to different noise (different bootstrap samples, random features), so the errors cancel; the shared real pattern survives.

Check yourself · 2 of 5

Your random forest went from 200 to 2,000 trees. Can it overfit more?

AnswerNo. More trees only make the average more stable; it costs time, not accuracy.

Check yourself · 3 of 5

Your XGBoost scores 0.98 train AUC and 0.83 test. Name three fixes.

AnswerLower the learning rate with early stopping; smaller trees (max_depth); bigger leaves / subsample / penalties.

Check yourself · 4 of 5

Data with 40 categorical columns like city and product ID. Which boosting library first?

AnswerCatBoost: it handles categories natively, without one-hot explosion.

Check yourself · 5 of 5

Boosting beats your logistic baseline by 0.002 AUC. Ship it?

AnswerProbably not: within noise, harder to explain, slower to run. Ship only when the gain matters to the business.
RememberAverage different trees → stable (forest).
Add trees that fix mistakes → strong (boosting).
Tune, validate, and beat a baseline.
